analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at a government-set benchmark rate plus four percentage points.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House Banking subcommittee and died at the end of the 102nd Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added a federal ceiling to the Truth in Lending Act: credit card interest rates could not exceed a benchmark rate set under the tax code plus 4 percentage points [S3]. It also would have required card issuers to clearly disclose the interest rate and any annual fee on initial credit card applications [S3]. It was introduced in November 1991 and referred to the House Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs Committee, which sent it to its consumer affairs subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households carrying credit card balances, who would pay less interest each month. In the early 1990s card rates commonly ran 18-19% while the benchmark rate the bill ties to sat far lower, so the ceiling would have forced issuers to cut rates on existing balances. Borrowers would also get the rate and any annual fee disclosed up front on applications [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps the annual percentage rate on credit card borrowing at 4 percentage points above the underpayment rate set under section 6621(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code, a government benchmark that in that era ran well below the 18-19% rates card issuers charged, so the ceiling would have lowered the maximum cost of carrying a balance.

Card issuers would have to clearly and conspicuously disclose the annual percentage rate and any annual or other fee on initial credit card applications, making the true cost of a card visible before a consumer signs up.
The ceiling takes effect January 1, 1992, and applies to extensions of credit obtained by use of a credit card.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and other companies that profit from the spread between the benchmark rate and the high rates they charge — would lose interest revenue. Issuers facing a capped interest rate would also have a stronger incentive to raise flat annual fees or tighten credit standards, so some consumers could pay more in fees or lose access to credit [S3].

drawbacks.text: A hard interest ceiling can squeeze credit availability: issuers who cannot price for risk by charging higher rates to riskier borrowers may respond by denying cards to people with weak credit, raising annual fees, or cutting rewards, so the borrowers the cap is meant to protect can end up paying more in fees or losing access.
The ceiling is tied to a tax-code benchmark rate that moves with market conditions, which makes the maximum card rate unpredictable over time for both issuers and borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households paying card rates in the high teens against a benchmark that was far lower, the cap would have delivered a direct, sizable reduction in interest costs. The honest cost is at the margin: capping rates limits issuers' ability to price risk, so some higher-risk borrowers could face higher fees or be denied credit, and the choice of benchmark makes the ceiling move with the market. On balance the bill's benefits to indebted households outweighed those costs, but it never received a hearing or vote, so no committee ever weighed them.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in November 1991 and referred to the House Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs Committee, which sent it to its consumer affairs subcommittee; nothing further happened before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Annunzio introduced the bill on November 14, 1991, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs.
Five days later, on November 19, 1991, the committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage, the last action ever recorded on it.
With only 3 cosponsors and no committee action, no markup, floor vote, or Senate consideration ever took place, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuing banks are better off, since the ceiling that would have cut their interest revenue never got a hearing or vote. Households carrying card balances continue paying the pre-cap rates.

for.name: Rep. Frank Annunzio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap credit card interest rates and add rate and fee disclosures on card applications.

for.name: 3 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to the Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage, and never reported it out; no markup or floor vote occurred before the Congress ended.

against.name: Credit card issuing banks
against.role: Industry affected by the rate ceiling
against.what_they_did: The credit card industry has long opposed federal interest rate ceilings, which would cut the interest revenue earned on high-rate card balances.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call shows where the full chamber stood.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and finance companies)
industries.note: The ceiling would cap the annual percentage rate card issuers can charge at a benchmark rate plus 4 points, cutting the interest revenue they earn on balances that typically carried much higher rates. Issuers would likely offset the cap with higher flat fees or tighter credit standards, so the industry's interest in defeating the bill ran directly against indebted cardholders.
Lower card rates could increase card usage and transaction volume over time, but the bill primarily targets issuer interest income rather than network fees, so the direct effect is modest.
